newsitem.title: USA: FAA inspector says he was overwhelmed at ValuJet.
newsitem.headline: FAA inspector says he was overwhelmed at ValuJet.

text.p: A U.S. aviation inspector told a hearing investigating the crash of a Valujet airplane on Thursday that the low-cost carrier's explosive growth kept him so busy he could not keep up with his job.

Robert Bruce, the Federal Aviation Administration inspector overseeing ValuJet, said he was certifying so many new aircraft and pilots he did not have time to review changes in the airline's operating procedures.

He said ValuJet had 40 pilots a month finishing its training programme at one point last year, taking up virtually all the time of one FAA inspector. But he said he never considered slowing the company's growth to get inspection procedures back on track.

The testimony came on the fourth day of a National Transportation Safety Board hearing into the crash of ValuJet Flight 592, which plunged into Florida's Everglades near Miami on May 11, killing all 110 passengers and crew on board.

"I am troubled by your workload," hearing chairman John Goglia said. "Any supervisor who is required to take home volumes of work to get the job done means something is wrong. You are not fulfilling your job and doing your duty to the flying public if you cannot see the forest because you're buried in the trees."

Relatives of passengers and crew killed in the crash who attended the session applauded Goglia's remarks, their first spontaneous outburst of emotion in the four days of the hearing. On Wednesday, a group of relatives accused the FAA of failing to oversee airlines properly and demanded the government require all airlines to install smoke detectors and fire suppression equipment in airplane cargo holds.
Investigators believe oxygen canisters improperly packed and loaded aboard the plane may have started or fuelled a fire in the DC-9's cargo hold.

Laura Sawyer, 22, whose grandparents were killed in the crash, said the testimony had "called into question" the ability of the FAA to inspect and regulate airlines. "It's obvious there are manpower problems," she said. "They are relying on the airlines too heavily."

Goglia told Bruce he was determined to correct the FAA's apparent shortage of inspectors. "Your job is to protect the public's interest in travel," he said. "If the system prevents you from accomplishing that, we're going to find out why and we're going to fix it."

Under insistent questioning, Bruce admitted he had not considered slowing ValuJet's growth by denying its requests to bring new aircraft and pilots on line until he had been able to approve revised operating procedures.
"They (planes and pilots) were more important to the company than my review of a new manual," he said.

Earlier, Bruce Butterworth, director of the FAA's Office of Civil Aviation Safety, said the agency had developed plans to increase surveillance of hazardous materials shipments aboard aircraft but had not implemented the programme to date.

Even with the addition of dozens of new inspectors, he said, the FAA would not be able to look for hazardous materials in every package put on an airplane. "You can't open all the boxes," he said. "It's physically impossible."
